blurb: Roles, the customer view, and the paths you will click for calling, contact center, and Dedicated Instance.

lessons.title: Administrator roles that matter here
lessons.summary: Full administrator and read-only administrator can cross-launch Dedicated Instance tools. Contact Center adds its own service administrator, and resource collections narrow what that person sees.
objectives: Separate a full admin from a Contact Center service admin
Remember who can open Web RTMT
Explain a resource collection

diagram.caption: Organization roles and Contact Center roles are related and not identical.

steps.label: Assign the Contact Center role
steps.detail: A full administrator can assign the Contact Center Service Administrator role.
steps.inspect: Customer or external user, with the limits in the roles article

steps.label: Configure the service
steps.detail: The role administers Contact Center features in Control Hub and the Management Portal and handles license and activation tasks.
steps.inspect: Not the same as a calling-only admin

steps.label: Monitor DI
steps.detail: Partner Sales Full Admin, and customer Full or Read-only admins, can cross-launch Web RTMT for Dedicated Instance.

steps.label: See a subset
steps.detail: A user profile can hold up to five resource collections. Flow Designer and Analyzer then show only those queues.

paragraphs: Cisco documents a Contact Center Service Administrator who can administer Contact Center features and perform user tasks such as sending an activation email and assigning Contact Center licenses.
The roles article is the source for which organization roles may assign that service role. Do not invent a 'queue admin' that the table does not list.

cite.label: Contact Center administrator roles

paragraphs: Resource collections hold resources such as queues. Assigning them to a user profile limits Control Hub, Flow Designer, Analyzer, and the supervisor view to those resources.
Cisco says you can assign up to five resource collections to a user profile. A person with a collection is a delegated administrator even if they also have an edit permission.

fault.symptom: An admin tries to attach a trunk before a location exists and the task stalls.

lessons.title: Users, workspaces, and numbers
lessons.summary: A person, a workspace, and a virtual line are three different places a number can live. The license decides which of those you are allowed to create.
objectives: Put the number on a location first
Choose user versus workspace
Know who can host a virtual line

diagram.caption: Users and workspaces both take numbers. They do not take the same licenses.

flow.title: Give a new hire a number

steps.label: Own the number
steps.detail: Numbers belong to a location. The location also holds the emergency address context.
steps.inspect: Location main number and caller ID

steps.label: Assign the user
steps.detail: Assign a calling license, then the number and extension.
steps.inspect: Professional if they need the full matrix

steps.label: Or a place
steps.detail: A lobby phone is a workspace. The workspace license is a single device.
steps.inspect: Do not expect the Webex App

steps.label: Only if Professional
steps.detail: The matrix marks virtual lines on Professional, one per Pro license, and not on Standard or Workspace.

sections.h: Shared lines are a Professional feature
paragraphs: The matrix allows a Professional user or Professional workspace to share lines, with 35 in the shared-line row. Standard and Workspace are No.

A shared line across locations has emergency consequences: the selected line's location decides emergency routing, and HELD is a device function that does not by itself force RedSky if that line's location is not enabled.

cite.label: Shared lines and virtual lines across locations

paragraphs: The ECBN article warns that some workspaces block inbound PSTN. Emergency callback is special: Webex Calling allows a callback that carries an emergency priority header, and it relaxes the blocking rule for 60 minutes on the device that dialed.
That 60-minute window is not a substitute for a reachable callback number. Set the ECBN.

cite.label: Emergency Callback Number in Control Hub

quiz.why: The matrix marks soft clients N for Workspace.

quiz.why: The shared-line article says HELD is independent of the lines, and routing still depends on the line location.

lessons.title: SSO, tokens, and what not to paste
lessons.summary: SSO is an identity requirement for one sync path. API tokens are a different secret, with a 12-hour personal token that Cisco says not to use in production.
objectives: Reject personal tokens in production
Separate a bot from an integration
Connect SSO to Dedicated Instance sync

diagram.caption: Human SSO and API tokens solve different problems.

steps.label: Copy a personal token
steps.detail: Cisco says a personal access token expires 12 hours after you sign in to the developer portal.

steps.label: Do not use it
steps.detail: The getting-started guidance says personal tokens should not be used in production. Build an integration.

steps.label: Use a bot token
steps.detail: A bot acts as itself. In a group space it only sees messages that mention it.

steps.label: Turn on SSO
steps.detail: That is the Dedicated Instance directory-sync requirement, unrelated to the bot token.

paragraphs: The Webex developer pages describe three ways to call the API: a personal access token, a bot token, or an OAuth token from an integration.
A personal token acts as you and is short-lived. An integration is how an app acts for other users. A bot is its own user, with a badge in the client.

cite.label: Webex bots

paragraphs: Do not 'fix' a missing Dedicated Instance user by minting a bot. The deployment article's requirement is SSO for directory sync.
Do not paste any of these tokens into a lesson note or a screenshot.

cite.label: Dedicated Instance customer deployment models

fault.title: A bot that ignores the room
fault.symptom: The bot answers in 1:1 chat and stays silent in the project space.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: webhook messages:created, group space, no mention, no delivery.
fault.cause: The bots guide says group-space messages are visible to the bot only when it is mentioned.
fault.fix: Mention the bot, or move the workflow to a 1:1 space. Do not widen the bot to read the room; that is not how the API works.

fault.title: Muscle memory from Call Manager
fault.symptom: An admin looks for route patterns under Call Routing > Route/Hunt and never opens Control Hub dial plans.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC ticket: still in Unified CM admin, Webex location has no dial plan.
fault.cause: Webex Calling dial plans are a Control Hub object. Unified CM route patterns still exist, but only on the cluster that still owns those phones.
fault.fix: Use Calling > Call Routing > Dial Plans for Webex Calling destinations and trunks. Keep Unified CM patterns for phones that still register there.

lessons.title: A change log you can defend
lessons.summary: Write down the article, the path, and the object name before you change a location. Future you will not remember which trunk was the one trunk.
objectives: Log one trunk per premises location
Attach a URL
Keep the previous value

diagram.caption: A defensible change names the object, the path, and the source.

steps.label: Read the current PSTN
steps.detail: Write down Cisco Calling Plan, CCP, or the trunk name.

steps.label: Open the page
steps.detail: Paste the URL of the page you followed, not a memory of it.

steps.label: Save
steps.detail: Change one thing. A PSTN change and a dial-plan change on the same afternoon are two records.

steps.label: One call
steps.detail: Place a known call: an internal extension, an external number, and 933 if you touched emergency calling.

sections.h: The one-trunk rule belongs in the log
paragraphs: Cisco says you cannot choose more than one trunk for a location with premises-based PSTN. The same trunk may serve many locations.
If the log shows two trunks on one location, the design is already outside the documented model.

cite.label: Configure Webex Calling for your organization

sections.h: 933 is a test, not a drill for sport
paragraphs: The emergency calling article tells you to test with 933 before you route live emergency calls to RedSky or Intrado.
Logging a 933 test is part of the change, including the dispatchable address you expected to see.

cite.label: Enhanced emergency calling for Webex Calling

fault.title: Two trunks selected
fault.symptom: Outbound calls from one site use a random gateway.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: location Oak, trunks selected = 2, premises PSTN.
fault.cause: The product model is one trunk per premises location.
fault.fix: Pick the trunk that owns that site's PSTN or PBX, remove the other, and retest. Use route groups and dial plans when you need more than a single default path.
